summary: multipass is a password manager that keeps every entry in one encrypted text file, the store. An entry has a name, a secret, and a few optional fields such as username and otp. The name is only a label, so nothing in multipass knows which website an entry belongs to, and no program can ask it which entries fit the page it is showing.

This pull request adds one plan, docs/projects/websites/readme.md, at status: ready. It changes no code. The plan gives each entry a repeatable website field and adds multipass find <url>, which prints the names of the entries whose websites match a page. A later browser extension, and the Mac and iPhone app in the passkeys plan, would use that answer to offer the right login on the right site.

• Strict parsing. A website is split into scheme, host, port, and the rest by one fixed rule, and every form a browser would read differently, such as a user name before an @, a backslash, or percent-encoding in the host, is refused. So find and the browser always agree on which host a page is on.
  • Matching. A stored website matches a page on the same host or a subdomain of it, with the same port, and never from a stored https address to an http page. A leading www. is ignored when the hosts are compared for equality, but never widens the subdomain test. This needs no Public Suffix List, the large, often-updated list of domain suffixes that whole-site matching would require.
  • Hints. When nothing matches, find names entries that share only the page's root domain on stderr, with the command that would add the page's scheme, host, and port, and never treats them as matches.
  • Store format. The field needs a new multipass <n> header. The plan builds on the mergeable store, takes format 4, and leaves renumbering the passkeys draft, which also claims 4, to the change that builds websites.
  • Deferred. The browser extension and per-site password rules get plans of their own later.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Store format. The number in the store's first line, multipass <n>. The repository changes the store text only by bumping it, so an older multipass refuses a store it cannot read.
  • Authority. The part of a URL after :// and before the path: the host and an optional port, and sometimes a user name and password before an @.
  • Root domain. The plan's short rule for a site's registered name: the last two labels of a host, or three after a country code's co, com, and similar.
  • Mergeable store. The store-merge plan: each entry records when it changed, and copies from two Macs merge entry by entry, the newer version winning.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
The first review, at dcf0ba8, opened three findings, all fixed at this head:

  • The plan never said where a URL's host ends, so https://bank.example@evil.example could have matched the bank's entry. § 2.1 now defines the split and refuses the confusing forms.
  • Removing www. before the subdomain test let a stored www. host match every subdomain of the bare host. Step 4 now ignores www. for equality only.
  • The format list that AGENTS.md would point to named format 4 as the passkey field. The note will now record formats 4 and 5 itself.

The second review, at 4343f5c, found the plan clean after it merged main and took all eight earlier suggestions, and it made two new ones. This head takes the first: the @ check runs before every other rule, so no error repeats a refused value that might hold a password. The second, giving find an exit status other than 1 for errors, still stands. The review of this head is clean.

groups.title: The websites plan
groups.kicker: A repeatable website field, the parsing and matching rules, and the format it needs
intro: The plan is the whole change. Read it in section order: § 2.1 defines the field, how a value is normalized, and how it is parsed, § 2.2 the matching rule and the root-domain hints, § 2.3 the commands and how a change merges, § 2.4 the store format number, and § 2.5 the files the change that builds it will touch.

Hold two things in mind while reading. First, the parsing and matching rules are the plan's security boundary: whatever website::matches accepts is a page where a later extension offers your password, so read each rule in § 2.1 and § 2.2 for a look-alike or attacker-controlled page that it lets through. Second, the plan builds on the mergeable store, which is not on main yet: the example in § 2.1 shows its modified line, and § 2.3 stamps each change through its Store::stamp.

checks.text: The plan's one open question, how strictly a website matches, is recorded as decided by the owner. The browser extension and per-site password rules are explicitly deferred, so no open question blocks status: ready.

files.note: The new plan: the website field, find, the parsing, matching, and hint rules, and the store format it takes.

checks.text: This list is what keeps find and a browser agreeing on the host. Read it against the forms a browser repairs: a tab or newline inside the address is a control character, which the Allowed values row refuses, and a host outside ASCII is refused, so only the xn-- form a browser reports can be stored or matched. The @ rule runs first, and no error names a refused value that holds an @, because the text before it may be a password.
Step 4 strips www. only for the equality test. The subdomain test uses the stored host as written, so a stored www.host.example matches host.example but not anyone.host.example.
The mergeable-store plan's format table names format 4 as the passkey field and becomes a completed record once that plan ships, so this row has the AGENTS.md note record formats 4 and 5 itself.
